title: Revisiting Stigma Attributions and Reactions to Stigma: Replication Registered Report of Weiner et al. (1988) With Extensions Examining New Stigmas and Stigma Origin Categorization

source.title: Revisiting Stigma Attributions and Reactions to Stigma: Replication Registered Report of Weiner et al. (1988) With Extensions Examining New Stigmas and Stigma Origin Categorization

studies.title: Replication and extensions · Stigma judgments
studies.description: One randomized experiment with three information conditions and fourteen repeated stigma targets.

nodes.title: How do explanations of stigma shape willingness to help?

fields.label: How do explanations of stigma shape willingness to help?
fields.value: This registered report revisits Weiner et al. (1988): perceived responsibility may shape sympathy, anger and helping intentions. It repeats Experiment 2 with a redesigned between-person information manipulation, adds four stigma targets and directly checks the assumed physical versus mental-behavioral categories.

fields.label: Attribution, affect and helping predictions
fields.value: Mental-behavioral targets were predicted to seem less stable and more controllable, evoke more anger and less sympathy, liking and helping. Uncontrollability, positive affect and helping were predicted to correlate, with affect–helping strongest. Controllability information was predicted to increase responsibility/blame/anger and reduce positive affect/helping.

nodes.title: Three randomized information conditions, fourteen repeated targets

fields.label: Three randomized information conditions, fourteen repeated targets
fields.value: Participants received no onset information, controllable-onset information or uncontrollable-onset information for all targets. Physical versus mental-behavioral category was repeated within participants and assigned analytically using the original classification. Unlike the 1988 design, controllability information was genuinely between participants.

fields.label: 804 US online participants
fields.value: Of 851 who began, 46 did not pass consent/verification and one reported being under 18, leaving 804. Recruitment used MTurk through CloudResearch. Analysis emphasizes completers; the prespecified additional exclusion sensitivity was conditional on failing replication and was not applied.

nodes.title: Ten original stigmas plus four extensions

fields.label: Ten original stigmas plus four extensions
fields.value: Targets include Alzheimer’s disease, blindness, cancer, heart disease, paraplegia, PTSD, AIDS, child abuse, drug abuse and obesity; diabetes, stroke, major depressive disorder and anxiety disorder are additions. Updated wording uses sympathy rather than pity and specifies US Americans and onset controllability.

nodes.title: Rate each target, then categorize its origin

fields.label: Rate each target, then categorize its origin
fields.value: After consent and eligibility checks, participants were assigned an information condition. Stigma order was randomized; dependent-variable order was fixed. Eight 0–8 ratings per target were followed by physical/mental-behavioral categorization in randomized order, then funneling questions, demographics and debriefing.

fields.label: Reported judgments, not observed helping
fields.value: The eight ratings measure changeability, responsibility, blame, sympathy, anger, liking, donation willingness and assistance willingness. A ninth response categorizes origin. These are reported tendencies; the study does not directly observe charitable donations or assistance behavior.

nodes.title: Separate category, correlation and information tests

fields.label: Separate category, correlation and information tests
fields.value: Matching category proportions were tested against 50%. Control-only repeated-measures ANOVAs compared stigma categories; correlations used both category averages per respondent. Mixed 2×2 ANOVAs compared controllable versus uncontrollable information; additional 2×3 analyses including control were exploratory. The paper contrasts replication effect intervals with original estimates.

nodes.title: Most categories match, with three important exceptions

fields.label: Most categories match, with three important exceptions
fields.value: Participants agreed with 11 of 14 classifications. Alzheimer’s disease (h=−.06,95% CI[−.23,.11]) and obesity (h=−.13,CI[−.30,.04]) were mixed; AIDS was predominantly categorized as physical, contrary to the original assignment (h=−1.05,CI[−1.22,−.88]).

nodes.title: Category averages reproduce the predicted attribution differences

fields.label: Category averages reproduce the predicted attribution differences
fields.value: In the no-information condition, mental-behavioral targets seemed more changeable (d=2.26), more responsibility-attracting (d=1.28) and more blame-attracting (d=1.20), all p<.001. These category summaries do not mean every individual stigma follows the pattern.

nodes.title: Affect is most strongly associated with helping

fields.label: Affect is most strongly associated with helping
fields.value: Helping correlated most with positive affect (r=.57,95% CI[.51,.63]), compared with physical source (r=.21,CI[.13,.29]) and uncontrollability (r=.26,CI[.18,.34]), all p<.001. These pooled category-average associations do not establish mediation causally.

nodes.title: Controllability information shifts all seven predicted judgments

fields.label: Controllability information shifts all seven predicted judgments
fields.value: Between information conditions, responsibility and blame effects were partial eta-squared .35 and .33; sympathy .06, anger .04, liking .03, donations .04 and assistance .04, all p<.001. Category-by-information interactions were nonsignificant for blame(p=.090), liking(.605), donations(.857) and assistance(.737), while responsibility, sympathy and anger interactions were significant.

nodes.title: Stability does not uniformly explain sympathy or helping

fields.label: Stability does not uniformly explain sympathy or helping
fields.value: In the control condition changeability correlated with responsibility(r=.50) and blame(r=.47), both p<.001, but not sympathy or helping. The paper also reports individual-target exceptions to the broad source dichotomy; these qualifications coexist with its overall replication conclusion.

nodes.title: Broad replication with a less simple stigma taxonomy

fields.label: Broad replication with a less simple stigma taxonomy
fields.value: The authors find overall consistency with the attribution–affect–help framework, generally smaller effects than the original, and evidence that perceived onset control is not determined solely by the physical/mental-behavioral label. The revised information design and added targets are explicit extensions.

nodes.title: Population, target ambiguity and unmeasured explanations

fields.label: Population, target ambiguity and unmeasured explanations
fields.value: The online US sample does not establish cross-cultural generality. Dangerousness and perceived suffering may explain some responses; respondents sometimes interpreted child abuse as referring to victims rather than perpetrators. The authors caution that their findings concern reactions to socially undesirable conditions under their particular stigma definition.

evidence.quote:
Participants
We recruited participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk
(MTurk) using the CloudResearch platform (Litman et al.,
2017). Of the 851 participants who began the survey, 46 did
not proceed beyond the consent and verification steps (see
the ‘Design and Procedure’ subsection), and one participant
reported an age below 18 and therefore did not meet the
minimum age requirement, resulting in a final sample of
804 participants.

Replication Hypotheses
3 Compared to physically based stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas are perceived to be less stable.
4 Compared to physically based stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas are perceived to be more onset-controllable.
5a Compared to physically based stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas elicit less sympathy.
5b Compared to physically based stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas elicit more anger.
5c Compared to physically based stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas elicit less liking.
5d Compared to physically based stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas elicit less charitable donations.
5e Compared to physically based stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas elicit less assistance.
6 Physical stigmas, perceived onset uncontrollability, positive affective reactions, and help-giving tendencies are positively correlated.
7 Among the positive correlations between physical stigmas, perceived onset uncontrollability, positive affective reactions, and help-giving
tendencies, the correlation between positive affective reactions and help-giving is the strongest.
8 Higher perceived controllability of a stigma leads to increased perceived responsibility, blame, and anger, and decreased liking and
sympathy towards the stigmatized individual, and decreased tendencies to provide personal assistance and donations.

Our experimental design manipulated controllability in-
formation with three outcomes: 1) control condition with
no information on stigma onset controllability, 2) condition
with stigma controllability information, and 3) condition
with stigma uncontrollability information (See Table S12 in
the supplementary materials for descriptions). Participants
were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions. The
order of dependent variables was consistent across all stig-
mas, but the display order of the stigmas was randomized.
Participants rated the following 14 stigmas: Alzheimer’s
disease, blindness, cancer, heart disease, paraplegia, dia-
betes, stroke, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), ac-
quired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), child abuse,
drug abuse, obesity, major depressive disorder (MDD), and
anxiety disorder. Table 8 provides a summary of the repli-
cation and extension experimental design.
Participants rated each stigma separately on several fac-
tors, and in the two information conditions, they were also
presented with information on the stigmas before making
the ratings. Overall, each participant made 126 ratings (9
questions for each of the 14 stigmas). At the end of the
experiment, participants answered several funneling ques-
tions, provided their demographic information, and were
debriefed.

(Physical or mental-behavioral)
To ensure attentiveness, we first introduced participants
with an attention check asking them to indicate which
stigma they were currently rating. Participants then re-
sponded to eight questions per stigma: 1) perceived sta-
bility (changeability), 2) perceived onset controllability for
a stigma: responsibility and blame, 3) three questions on
affective reactions towards the individuals with the partic-
ular condition: sympathy, anger, liking, 4) two questions
on help-giving tendencies: charitable donation and assis-
tance. Questions on categorizing the fourteen stigmas by
source were grouped and presented in random order after
participants had responded to the above eight questions per
stigma. Such arrangement ensured the extension’s robust-
ness in verifying if perceived sources of stigmas influence
perceptions of stigmas, as hypothesized in Weiner et al.
(1988). If the manipulation was presented before the above
eight questions, it might reinforce participants’ pre-exist-
ing beliefs that influence their perceptions of stigmas, and
such being salient would nullify the experimental manip-
ulation. Except for perceived stigma origin, all dependent
variables were on a 9-point scale anchored at the extremes
(e.g., 0 - Not responsible at all; 8 - Entirely responsible).
Deviations from the original

Building on constructive peer reviewer feedback, we im-
proved the experimental design to test for the causal effects
of controllability information on perceptions of stigmas. In
our replication, the IV controllability information was truly
between-subjects (i.e., participants either received no in-
formation, information that depicted all conditions as on-
set controllable, or all conditions as onset uncontrollable).
The authors of the target article generated twelve ques-
tionnaire formats based on three order factors: 1) stigma
display order, 2) dependent variable display order, and 3)
balancing the controllability and uncontrollability informa-
tion. They concluded that display order did not impact re-
sults. Thus, there was no true randomization of stigma dis-
play order, and using the original’s experimental design in
controllability information display resulted in specific stig-
mas to be contrasted against specific others regarding con-
trollability information (see summary in Table 1). We con-
ducted full randomization of the stigmas’ display order and
fixed the order of the dependent variables to be consistent
across all stigmas for all participants.
Next, we changed the questionnaire to address study de-
sign issues, such as modifying the measurement scale (see
Table 1). Moreover, we instructed participants that their
ratings should be made in consideration of other US Amer-
icans with a particular condition, as perceived stigma on-
set controllability could vary across different countries and
cultures. We also specified that controllability ratings per-
tained to onset-controllability, as the original study did not
specify to participants whether the judgments pertained to
onset or offset-controllability.
Lastly, we made changes to the wording. “Sympathy”
was used in our survey to replace “pity”. We also changed
the wording of different stigma labels. As “Vietnam War
syndrome” seemed to be outdated, we changed the stigma
label to “post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD),” which we
thought was more generalizable and fitting for current
times. In addition, we used the terms “individuals/people
with obesity” and “individuals/people with AIDS” to not
perpetuate stigma in research.

Data analysis strategy
Extension
We counted the number and percentage of responses in
which participants’ categorizations of the stigmas by ori-
gin matched with the researchers’ assumptions. We then
conducted a two-sample proportions test on the matching
rates against a 50-50 split which indicates random answer-
ing or neutrality. All analyses outlined in this section in-
cluded the four newly added stigmas - diabetes, stroke,
MDD, and anxiety disorder.
Replication: As in the original
Following Weiner et al. (1988), we first focused on the
no information (control) condition (n = 257) and conducted
one-way repeated measures ANOVAs to compare the seven
physically based versus the seven mental-behavioral stig-
mas.
Replication: Improvement from the original
For the correlation and multiple regression analyses,
Weiner et al. (1988) only included ratings from eleven or
twelve participants per stigma to examine associations be-
tween stigma source, perceived onset uncontrollability,
positive affect, and help-giving tendencies. In other words,
the original analyses included half of the participants’ rat-
ings on physically based stigmas and half of the remaining
participants’ ratings on mental-behavioral stigmas. Unlike
the original, we included all participants’ ratings on both
sources of stigmas (i.e., 257 x 2 = 514 responses) in our cor-
relation and multiple regression analyses.
We used 2 (source - within-subject: physically based and
mental-behavioral stigmas) x 2 (controllability - between-
subject: controllable and uncontrollable) mixed ANOVAs to
compare perceived controllability, affective reactions, and
help-giving judgments towards stigmas in the controllabil-
ity condition (n = 267) versus in the uncontrollability infor-
mation (n = 280).
Exploratory analyses

Exclusions
As pre-registered, our reporting focuses on the full sam-
ple of participants who completed the study. We predeter-
mined exclusions that we planned to examine in case we
failed to find support for our predictions. Given that the
overall replication was successful, we did not proceed with
this plan.

We conducted a
two-sample proportions test evaluating the matching rates
against a 50-50 split and found that on average participants
tended to agree with the researchers’ categorizations of 11
of the 14 stigmas (all hs ≥ 0.66 with 95% confidence inter-
vals excluding 0, see Table 10).
As for the remaining three stigmas, there were mixed
perceptions on the categorizations of Alzheimer’s disease
(h = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.23, 0.11]), and obesity (h = -0.13, 95%
CI [-0.30, 0.04]). Most participants agreed that AIDS was
physically based (h = -1.05, 95% CI [-1.22, -0.88]).
Thus, we found support for Hypotheses 1b - 1g, 2a, 2c,
2d, 2f, and 2g and failed to find support for Hypotheses 1a,
2b, and 2e.

Hypothesis 3: Perceived changeability differs by
stigma source
We conducted a one-way repeated measures ANOVA and
found support for a main effect of stigma source on per-
ceived changeability (η2
p = .84, 90% CI [.80, .86]) (Table 12;
Figure 2). That is, perceived changeability of mental-behav-
ioral stigmas was higher (M = 4.96, SD = 1.17) than that
of physically based stigmas (M = 2.48, SD = 1.12; t(256) =
36.21, p < .001; d = 2.26 [2.02, 2.53]). Thus, we found sup-
port for Hypothesis 3, which predicted that mental-behav-
ioral stigmas are perceived to be less stable.
Hypothesis 4: Perceived controllability of stigma
onset differs by stigma source
We found support for differences between the two
sources of stigmas in terms of ratings on our two indexes
of perceived controllability: perceived responsibility (η2
p
= .62, 90% CI [.56, .68]), and blame (η2
p = .59, 90% CI
[.52, .65]) (Table 12; Figure 3). Specifically, individuals with
mental-behavioral stigmas were perceived to be more re-
sponsible for their condition (M = 3.43, SD = 1.26) compared
to individuals with physically based stigmas (M = 2.07, SD =
1.08; t(256) = 20.52, p <.001; d = 1.28 [1.12, 1.45]). Individu-
als with mental-behavioral stigmas were also blamed more
for their condition (M = 3.20, SD = 1.30) compared to those
with physically based stigmas (M = 1.90, SD = 1.10; t(256) =
19.19, p <.001; d = 1.20 [1.04, 1.36]).
In sum, we found support for Hypothesis 4 that mental-
behavioral stigmas are perceived to be more onset-control-
lable.
Hypothesis 5a - 5c:

Hypothesis 6 - 7: Correlations between stigma
source, perceived controllability, affective reactions,
and help-giving tendencies
We summarized the findings regarding Hypotheses 6 and
7 in Table 13. We included participants’ ratings of both
sources of stigmas in correlational and multiple regression
analyses.
Our analyses for these hypotheses followed the methods
used by Weiner et al. (1988). We first created a controlla-
bility index by adding ratings on responsibility and blame;
a positive affect index by subtracting anger ratings from
the sum of liking and sympathy ratings; a helping index by
adding ratings on tendencies to provide donation and assis-
tance. Lastly, we included the manipulated stigma source as
a categorical variable, with physically based stigmas coded
as 1 and mental-behavioral stigmas coded as 0 in the analy-
sis.
We conducted Pearson correlation analyses and found
support for Hypotheses 6 and 7. Judgments of help had the
strongest correlation with positive affect (r(512) = .57, 95%
CI [.51, .63]), with smaller effects for stigma source (r(512)
= .21, 95% CI [.13, .29]), and perceived uncontrollability
(r(512) = .26, 95% CI [.18, .34], p <.001) (all ps <.001) (see
Table 13), providing support for Hypotheses 6 and 7 with
similar effects.

Categorizing stigmas by source
Among all fourteen stigmas, participants’ categoriza-
tions of Alzheimer’s disease, AIDS, and obesity by origin
were either mixed or did not match researchers’ assump-
tions. Differences in perceptions might be due to the nature
of stigmas, which elicit stereotypes and knowledge struc-
tures adopted by the general public on a marked social
group (Hilton & von Hippel, 1996; Judd & Park, 1993;
Krueger, 1996). Thus, Alzheimer’s disease and obesity may
have elicited highly varied knowledge structures among
people, as suggested by recent research: Laditka et al.
(2012) revealed that certain ethnic groups in America at-
tribute Alzheimer’s disease to mental-health related fac-
tors, such as anxiety or stress. Others perceive disease or
heredity as causes. As for obesity, Puhl and Liu (2015) found
that around half of the US American participants viewed
the condition as a disease. Lastly, AIDS is strongly associ-
ated with ideas of contagion (Relf et al., 2015) to the ex-
tent that discrimination against individuals with AIDS can
be largely attributed to false beliefs about its transmission
(von Collani et al., 2010). Thus, AIDS, portrayed as a dis-
ease that “can be caught,” might be primarily understood as
a condition arising from somatic abnormalities.
Four new stigmas

Perceived stability and controllability
In the no information condition, AIDS elicited high (i.e.,
above overall average) ratings on perceived controllability
and low (i.e., below overall average) ratings on perceived
changeability. However, it did not elicit particularly high
ratings on sympathy. Correlation analyses revealed that
changeability was positively associated with responsibility
(r(512) = .50, 95% CI [.40, .59], p <.001), and blame (r(512) =
.47, 95% CI [.37, .56], p <.001). However, perceived change-
ability was not associated with ratings on sympathy and
helping tendencies. Although PTSD, MDD, and anxiety dis-
order were perceived as more changeable than AIDS, those
three conditions elicited lower ratings on perceived con-
trollability and higher ratings on sympathy. The above find-
ings showed that, contrary to the review by Weiner (1986),
greater perceived stability does not necessarily evoke
greater pity compared to unstable states and may not offset
the effect of higher perceived controllability.
Changes and discrepancies in stigma perceptions

Limitations
Constraints on generalizability
Definition of “stigma”
Weiner et al. (1988) followed the definitions by Jones
et al. (1984) and Goffman (1963), conceptualizing stigma
as “a mark or sign for perceived conditions of deviations
from the norm” and a bearer of stigma is viewed as “gen-
erally limited or undesirable.” The target article concluded
that stigmas “represent negative outcomes or unwanted ef-
fects.” We followed the original’s conceptualization, which
primarily portrayed stigmas as conditions undesirable or
limiting in society. However, there have been multiple def-
initions of stigma since Jones and Goffman, including con-
notating stigma with discrimination (Link & Phelan, 1999,
2001). Thus, the current study may be better understood as
“an attributional analysis of reactions to socially undesir-
able conditions,” and our findings may not apply to other
definitions of stigma.
Participants
Stigma is a social construction and so may vary across
different social contexts. It is possible that the effects of the
attribution-affect-help judgment model may hold across
cultures (Rudolph et al., 2004), yet what is considered a
negative characteristic is likely influenced to some extent
by cultural norms and ideologies (Corrigan et al., 2014). For
example, anti-fat attitudes may vary across different cul-
tures (Crandall et al., 2001), and depression may be viewed
more negatively in cultures with a stronger social domi-
nance orientation (Shamblaw et al., 2015).
We conducted our data collection with an online US
American sample, whereas the original study conducted
data collection in-person with US American and Canadian
student populations (see deviation documented in Table 9),
and yet we concluded that the findings were very consis-
tent. Further studies are needed to directly test generaliz-
ability to other populations by rerunning the study in other
cultures and contexts.
Materials and stimuli
Findings on drug abuse may suggest a confounding fac-
tor influencing participants’ positive affect and helping
judgments towards stigmas - perceived dangerousness. Per-
ceptions of uncontrollability might have little effect when
the individual is believed to be causing suffering to other
people (Jahnke et al., 2014), which elicits strong feelings of
anger and reduced sympathy (Liekens et al., 2012). Aside
from being perceived as responsible for their condition, in-
dividuals with substance use disorders may also be per-
ceived as violent towards others (Barry et al., 2014;
Humphreys, 2017), further eliciting little positive affect and
helping tendencies from participants.
Expanding on the above, the unlikely combination of
ratings on child abuse also points to the potentially con-
founding effects of perceived dangerousness and areas of
improvement in our study. In line with our predictions on
child abuse being an outlier, some of our participants in-
dicated in the funneling questions that they were unsure if
they were making ratings for the abusers, or the victims.
The valence of the behavioral cause, or desirability of the
action leading to the condition, can also influence reactions
of anger and subsequent helping judgments towards stig-
mas (Dijker & Koomen, 2003). The more an individual’s be-
havior is seen as incongruent with societal norms or partic-
ipants’ goals, the more it is negatively evaluated and causes
anger (Ortony et al., 1988). Thus, individuals involved with
drug addiction and child abuse, which have high perceived
dangerousness and naturally incur serious violations of so-
cietal norms, elicit little sympathy from participants. Al-
though the perceived dangerousness of obesity is low, the
condition appears to go against socio-cultural norms of
valuing health and defining personal success based on an
individual’s adoption of healthy practices (Crawford, 2006),
ultimately eliciting rejection from others.
Perceived suffering may also influence participants’
judgments of stigma, as the perception of another person’s
physical or psychological suffering arouses sympathy and

Conclusion
In this Registered Report, we conducted a well-powered
independent close replication of Weiner et al. (1988) with
new extensions. Our replication findings are largely consis-
tent with original findings, although effects are generally
smaller. From our extension findings, we discovered that
perceived controllability of stigma onset might not be
solely contingent on stigma source, and participants may
classify stigmas in ways that extend beyond the dichotomy
of physically based versus mental-behavioral. We found
support for associations between perceived stigma onset
controllability, affective reactions, and helping tendencies
for stigmatized individuals. We call for future directions
to address the discussed limitations and to further inves-
tigate associations between classifications of stigma, per-
ceived controllability, affective reactions, and helping judg-
ments.
